e.t: Agallim is a proper name, referring to a specifically named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. Its exact identity is not further defined by the available lexical information. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Isaiah 15:8. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain what Agallim refers to in that passage; the name itself supplies identification, not a broader abstract meaning.

Adama, also called Athama, is a proper name for a place. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a geographical name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs six times, all in six Old Testament verses, including passages in Genesis, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Hosea. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise role in each passage cannot be described further; its established meaning here is the place-name “Adama; Athama.”

This noun means “immortality”: life that does not end in death. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it appears seven times, all in Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. It names the condition or hope of continuing life, rather than an action someone performs. The surrounding passage determines how the word applies in each occurrence, but its central meaning remains the state of being deathless or everlasting.

This adjective describes something that is not to be swallowed. It presents the idea of an item that should remain undigested or not be taken down, rather than something suitable for consumption. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Job 20:18. The word’s basic meaning is clear from its direct definition, while the precise force of the description in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. It belongs to the Greek Old Testament vocabulary and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament word.

This word means “cock,” the male bird of the chicken. It is a noun naming that bird rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 5:23. The word’s basic meaning is therefore specific and concrete: it identifies a cock. The precise significance of its use in that verse must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “leap up” or “start up,” describing sudden upward movement or rising into action. It can portray someone springing up quickly rather than simply standing or moving gradually. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in four separate verses. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on what or who is rising and the surrounding sentence.

This LXX Greek verb means “kindle”: to set something alight or cause it to burn. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this LXX corpus, including uses in 2 Chronicles, Psalms, Jeremiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being kindled and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “come eye to eye”: to meet another directly, face to face. Its focus is a personal encounter, not a general state or abstract condition. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 12:14. Because the verse text is not included here, its precise role in that passage cannot be stated beyond this central sense. The word presents one person meeting another directly and personally.

This noun means “piercing”—the act or result of being pierced. It is a noun naming this action or result, rather than a person, place, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Hosea 9:13. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s particular force in that passage must be understood from its context; its basic lexical sense remains “piercing.”

This noun means “response”: something said or given in answer to a question, statement, or situation. It describes the act or substance of answering rather than the person who answers. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 13 times, including several occurrences in Job. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains an answer offered in return.

e.h: To Defend or Make a Defense
e.t: This Greek verb means to defend oneself or another, or to make a defense. It describes giving an answer or presenting a case when facing accusation, challenge, or opposition. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs three times, so it is an uncommon word in this corpus. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding words and situation, but its central idea is a spoken or reasoned defense rather than a physical act of protection.

This Greek LXX noun means “silver piece; money.” It refers to silver as a valuable material and to money used in buying, selling, or paying. The word can therefore describe the substance itself or its role as currency, depending on the sentence. It occurs 352 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing broad use for ordinary wealth and payment. Its exact sense in a particular verse comes from the surrounding context.

This noun means “plowing,” the work of turning and preparing soil for cultivation. It names an agricultural activity rather than a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 45:6. That single occurrence shows that the word belongs to the ordinary vocabulary of farming, but the reference alone does not provide enough surrounding text here to explain any further contextual emphasis. Its basic meaning remains the agricultural work of plowing the ground.

Asedoth, also rendered Asithoth, is a proper name rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. Its form is preserved as a name in the Greek Old Testament, so the available meaning does not extend beyond identifying this named entity. It occurs seven times in the Greek LXX, appearing in Deuteronomy and Joshua. Its precise identity or significance in any particular passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding text.

This adjective means “intolerable” or “insufferable”: it describes something that cannot be endured or borne. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 9:10. The word’s basic force is a strong negative judgment about the severity or burden of something, rather than a description of a person, action, or object by itself. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

gl: grievous of tongue; speaking a foreign language
d: grievous of tongue; speaking a foreign language

e.t: This adjective describes someone as “grievous of tongue” or as “speaking a foreign language.” It points to speech that is difficult or burdensome in relation to the tongue, with the wording also covering a person who speaks another language. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 3:5. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its lexical sense centers on difficult or unfamiliar speech.

This verb means “confirm”—to make something firm, certain, or established. It expresses the act of affirming or strengthening something so that it can be relied upon. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Psalms, showing a focused use rather than a broad range of recorded contexts. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains the same: confirming or making secure what is being addressed.

This proper name identifies Bethel, also rendered “Vithil.” It is a place-name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:32. The name itself does not provide the details of that passage’s setting or significance; those depend on the surrounding verse and context. Its lexical identity is therefore straightforward: it names Bethel, with Vithil given as an alternate rendering.

Bochori, also rendered Vokhori, is a proper name rather than a word describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person connected with the events recorded in 2 Samuel 20. The name occurs eight times, all within that chapter. Its meaning is therefore primarily its use as a personal designation; the available information does not provide a separate definition or explain the name’s etymology.

Gadalia is a proper name, also rendered Gathalia. It identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 10:18. The available wording supports recognizing it as a personal name, but does not provide a broader definition or meaning for the name itself. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Godollathi is a personal name, also represented as Gothollathi, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. As a proper noun in the Greek LXX, it functions to identify an individual by name. It occurs twice in this corpus, both in 1 Chronicles: once in 25:4 and once in 25:29. The available information establishes the name’s identity and usage, but does not provide a further lexical meaning.

Dabōr, also written Thavor, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 6:58. Because it functions as a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points to a particular person or place named in that passage, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific reference. The form itself does not provide a broader abstract meaning.

Denethi is a proper name, appearing as “Denethi; Thenethi.” It identifies a named individual or designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs only once, at 1 Chronicles 3:18. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the precise person or role identified by the name must be determined from that passage itself. The name should therefore be understood as a specific biblical designation, not translated as an ordinary descriptive word.

This verb means to “give a public address”—to speak openly before a gathered audience. It describes public speaking rather than private conversation, and its emphasis is on addressing people directly. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Proverbs and once in 4 Maccabees. The surrounding passage determines the particular purpose or subject of the address, but the word itself focuses on the public act of speaking.

This word means “because” or “that,” linking a statement with its reason or explaining what is being said. It commonly introduces the cause behind an action, claim, or situation, so readers can understand why something is true or happens. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 314 times, showing that it is a regular connective word rather than a rare or specialized term. Its precise role in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding words.

This word means “twice”. It is an adverb that describes something happening two times or being repeated on two occasions. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it appears 16 times, showing a consistent numerical meaning rather than a broader symbolic one. It can describe repeated actions, repeated events, or a doubled occurrence, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is repeated. Its use extends from Genesis through 1 Maccabees.

This noun means “unlucky day”: a day viewed as bringing bad fortune or unfavorable circumstances. It names the day itself rather than describing a person or action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:6. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is a day considered unlucky.

This Greek LXX noun means “sitting-place”: a place or seat connected with sitting. It names a location associated with sitting rather than an action or activity. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs six times across five verses, chiefly in 1 Samuel, with one occurrence in Deuteronomy. Its precise reference in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a place designated for sitting.

This Greek LXX verb means to decide finally or settle a matter. It describes bringing an issue to a definite conclusion rather than leaving it unresolved. As a verb, it expresses an action—someone determines an outcome or establishes a settlement. It occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including passages from Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Ezekiel, and the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means “squeeze out”: it describes forcing something out by applying pressure. It functions as an action word, naming what someone or something does rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 22 times in 21 verses, including Old Testament and deuterocanonical passages. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on what is being forced out and the surrounding sentence.

Elibema, also rendered Elivema, is a proper name for a person. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. In the Greek Septuagint, this name occurs seven times, all within Genesis 36. The available references show repeated use of the same name in that genealogy, but the name itself does not describe the person’s character or role. Those details must be understood from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

Enatos is a proper name, rendered “Enatos.” It functions as a personal or named designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general. Within the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 23 times across 22 verses, from Leviticus through 2 Maccabees. The word appears in Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, but the available lexical information identifies its name rather than explaining a broader descriptive meaning. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

ἐντομίς means an “incision” or “gash”: a cut made into the body. It is a noun describing the cut itself rather than the act of cutting. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in passages from Leviticus and Jeremiah. Its basic sense focuses on a bodily cut or wound. The surrounding verse determines how that cut functions in the passage, but the word itself names the physical incision or gash.

The word means “lodge”: a place for staying. As a noun, it names the lodging place itself, not the act of staying or a person who stays there. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 37 times across 35 verses, showing that it is used repeatedly for a place where people may stay. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.h: A Word for In Fit Time
e.t: This word is an adjective that describes a quality or condition. Its basic sense is “in fit time”. It describes something suited to the right moment or occurring at an appropriate time, rather than being early, late, or poorly timed. In this Greek Old Testament corpus, it appears four times, all in 2 Maccabees, so its meaning is focused and specific rather than broadly represented across many books. The surrounding verse determines what situation is being called timely.

This Greek LXX noun means “cutting on the surface; incision”—a cut made into or across a surface. It names the act or result of making such a cut, rather than describing a person or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, both in 2 Maccabees, appearing in 2 Maccabees 2:26 and 2:28. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains a surface cut or incision.

This adjective means “arable”: land that is suitable for cultivation or farming. It describes ground in terms of its usefulness for growing crops, rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Leviticus 13:48–49. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its precise role in either passage, but its basic sense remains land capable of being worked for agricultural purposes.

This Greek LXX adverb means “easily,” describing an action that can be done without much difficulty or effort. It tells how something happens rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including Proverbs, Wisdom, and 3 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains the same wherever it occurs, while the surrounding sentence determines exactly what is being done easily.

This LXX noun is associated with the meanings “his disaster” and “light.” It names rather than describes an action, since it functions as a noun. These two meaning phrases point to distinct possibilities, so the surrounding context is needed to determine which sense is intended in its single occurrence, Job 36:30. It appears only once within this Greek Old Testament corpus.

This word means “sheath,” a covering or case used to hold and protect a blade. It is a noun naming that object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs three times, in Exodus and Isaiah. Its basic meaning remains consistent wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse determines how the object functions in that particular passage.

Iabnēl, also given as Iavnil, is a proper name: it identifies a distinct named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The available lexical information preserves the name in these two forms but does not specify whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:11, so its precise referent belongs to that passage’s surrounding context.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named Iaēl, also rendered Iel. It is not a general description or action word, but a personal designation used in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs six times in six verses, all within Judges 4–5, from Judges 4:17 through Judges 5:24. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, while the word itself functions simply as the person’s name.

Iarin is a proper name, preserved as “Iarin” in the Greek Old Testament tradition. It does not function as a general word describing an action, quality, or object; it identifies a named entity in the text. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in Joshua 9:17 and once in 2 Samuel 20:26. Since the verse text is not provided here, the particular person or setting connected with the name must be determined from each passage.

Ieēla, also rendered Iila, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (the LXX), it occurs once, in Ezra 2:56. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide a further meaning or description, so it is best understood as the identifying name recorded in that passage.

Iōbab, also rendered Iovav, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs 12 times in 11 verses, from Genesis through Job, showing that it appears in several Old Testament genealogical and narrative settings. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on which person bearing this name is being mentioned.

This Greek LXX verb means “make up the face,” describing the act of adorning or arranging the face. It refers to an outward action involving facial appearance rather than an inner attitude or abstract idea. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, across Genesis, Psalms, and Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and how the action is being described.

Kana is a proper name for a place. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Genesis and specifically in Genesis 40:16 and 40:18. The name itself identifies the place rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. Because no verse text or surrounding passage is included here, the particular role of Kana in those verses cannot be explained further from the name alone.

Kariathsōphar, also rendered Kariathsofar, is a proper name for a place or settlement. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Judges 1:11. Because the available lexical information identifies it only as this name and does not provide the name’s underlying meaning, its significance here is its role as a geographic designation rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object.

This noun means "veil": a covering that hangs before or around a place or object, separating or concealing what lies beyond it. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used especially for the curtains associated with the tabernacle and other holy furnishings, so its ordinary sense is a physical cloth barrier or screen. The word occurs 38 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, most often in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding description.

This Greek LXX verb means “furnish” or “prepare.” It describes making something ready or supplying what is needed for its intended use. The word is used 27 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, so its basic idea applies in different settings without changing its central sense. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The surrounding sentence determines what is being furnished or prepared.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Kaphan” or “Kafan.” It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 18:27. Without the surrounding verse text, the name’s specific identity cannot be described further here, but its lexical function is clear: it serves as a personal or place name in that passage.

This noun means a “Laconian drinking-vessel,” referring to a cup or container used for drinking. It names a particular kind of vessel rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Esther and once in 3 Maccabees. The word’s precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its ordinary meaning remains a drinking vessel associated with Laconia.

This noun means “stone cutter’s tool,” naming an implement used for shaping or working stone. It refers to a physical tool rather than to the person who uses it or the work itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Psalm 73:6. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context, but the word’s basic meaning remains a tool employed in cutting or carving stone.

This word means “shiny,” describing something that has a bright, polished, or gleaming appearance. As an adjective, it adds this quality to a person, object, or surrounding scene rather than naming the thing itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, appearing once each in Judges, Nehemiah, and Isaiah. Its exact shade of meaning—whether bright, glossy, or richly gleaming—depends on the noun and surrounding verse, but its central idea is visible brightness or luster.

Maththanias is a proper name referring to a person named Maththanias. It functions as an identifying name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, once in 2 Kings 24:17 and once in 2 Chronicles 29:13. The name itself identifies the person, while the surrounding verse and passage determine which Maththanias is being mentioned and what is happening in each occurrence.

Maitebeēl, also rendered Metevil, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies an individual by name. This name occurs once in the LXX, in Genesis 36:39. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not establish an additional ordinary meaning or explain its possible name elements. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being identified there.

μάτην means “groundlessly; in vain.” It is an adverb describing an action, claim, or result as lacking a sound reason or producing no useful outcome. Rather than naming a person or object, it tells how something is done or what comes from it. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 23 times, describing futile or unjustified activity. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence.

Menelaos is a proper name referring to a particular man, rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it identifies a person named Menelaos. The name occurs 16 times, all in 2 Maccabees, from 2 Maccabees 4:23 through 13:7. Because no verse text or surrounding context is included, the name itself tells us who is being identified, while the specific actions, character, and role associated with him must be learned from each passage.

This verb means “apportion; allocate”—to assign something in separate portions or allot it to people or groups. It describes distributing what is available according to an assigned share. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs 33 times, showing that this basic action appears across many passages. The surrounding verse determines what is being assigned and who receives it.

This Greek LXX verb means “in suspense”: being held up, unsettled, or left waiting rather than moving to a settled outcome. It describes a state of suspension, whether involving a person, movement, or situation. The word occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is broader than one isolated passage. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording and context.

This verb means to remember or be mindful of someone or something. It can describe keeping a person, promise, need, or past act in mind, and it may also express a request that someone remember. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, it occurs 133 times, so it is used broadly rather than for one narrow kind of remembrance. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This noun means “field-mouse,” referring to a small rodent found in the land. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears seven times in six verses, with one occurrence in Leviticus and six in 1 Samuel. The word names the animal itself rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. Its precise significance in any verse comes from that passage’s wording and context.

This noun means “anything flowing; running water.” It refers to water in motion, such as water that streams or runs rather than remaining still. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented by the Septuagint, in Song of Songs 8:2. Its basic meaning is therefore focused and concrete: a flowing water source or stream. The surrounding verse determines how this image functions there, but the word itself identifies the water by its movement.

This word means “deputy” or “official,” referring to a person who holds an appointed position of responsibility. As a noun, it identifies someone serving in an authorized role rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at 1 Kings 4:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense points to a recognized officer or representative.

This Greek LXX noun means “living abroad”—residing away from one’s own country or homeland. It describes the condition of being settled in a foreign place rather than at home. The word occurs once in the Greek text of Wisdom, at Wisdom 18:3. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its exact emphasis in that occurrence must be understood from its context. Its central idea remains the experience or state of living away from home.

This adjective means “with the whole root.” It describes something that possesses or remains connected to an entire root, emphasizing completeness at the root rather than a partial or broken connection. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Job 4:7 and Proverbs 15:6. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is being whole or complete down to the root.

This Greek LXX noun means “partridge,” the name of a bird. It refers to the bird itself rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Jeremiah and once in Sirach. Those references establish its normal lexical sense, while the particular force of the word in either passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “pour over,” describing liquid being poured across or onto something. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, it occurs four times, including passages from 2 Chronicles, Jonah, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being poured and what receives it, but the central idea remains the spreading or covering movement of liquid over something.

This noun means “anything woven; web”—something formed by twining strands together. It can refer either to the woven material itself or to a web-like structure. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Exodus 28:14. The word’s basic sense is concrete and practical: it names an interconnected arrangement made through weaving or twining, rather than an action, person, or abstract quality.

gl: producing many at a birth; prolific
d: producing many at a birth; prolific

e.t: This adjective describes someone or something that produces many children in a single birth, so it means “producing many at a birth” or “prolific.” It speaks of abundant offspring rather than merely general productivity. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs twice, in Wisdom 4:3 and 4 Maccabees 15:5. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject being described.

gl: choose before others; choose by preference
d: choose before others; choose by preference

e.t: This verb means to choose someone or something before others, giving it preference. It describes an act of selecting one option as the preferred choice rather than treating all options alike. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Wisdom 7:8, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. Its basic idea remains clear: to place one choice ahead of competing choices. The precise force in Wisdom 7:8 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person called “Reēa” or “Rhia.” It is not a description of an action, quality, or object, but identifies an individual by name. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Ezra 2:47. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the name itself does not indicate the person’s role or significance in that passage.

Sabatha is a proper name, also given as Savatha. It functions as a personal or place name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, appearing in Genesis, Numbers, and 1 Chronicles. The available passages identify the name, but without their verse text they do not establish whether each occurrence refers to a person, a family, or a location. Its meaning is therefore best stated as the name “Sabatha” or “Savatha.”

Sami is a proper name, referring to a person or group identified by that name in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general description or action word, so its meaning is chiefly the identification of the named party. The name occurs three times in the Greek LXX, in two verses of Numbers 26. Its precise reference in those verses depends on the surrounding passage and the specific person or family being named.

Sanesar is a proper name used as a personal designation. Its meaning is simply “Sanesar,” rather than a descriptive word or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 3:18. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not provided here, the name’s specific role in that genealogy cannot be explained further; its lexical function is to identify the named individual.

Saraia, also rendered Sarea, is a proper name used for people in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies individuals rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The name appears twelve times in twelve Old Testament verses, especially in genealogical and historical passages in 1 Chronicles and Nehemiah, and also in Ezra and Jeremiah. Because it is a personal name, its meaning here is primarily identification: recognizing which person is being mentioned. The surrounding verse is needed to determine that individual’s particular role or place in the passage.

Saphi is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It is rendered “Saphi” and is also identified as “Safi.” In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this name occurs once, at 1 Samuel 30:28. Because it is a personal name, its meaning is primarily its role in identifying that individual; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s specific place in the passage.

This word is a personal name, rendered “Sērōn” or “Siron.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Maccabees, at 1 Maccabees 3:13 and 3:23. The exact significance of the person named depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself functions simply as a proper name.

This word means “carpenter’s axe” or “axe,” the hand tool used for cutting or shaping wood. It is a noun naming the tool itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 44:12, and its ordinary meaning is clear from the short definition and translation as “axe.” The word identifies a practical woodworking implement rather than an action or quality. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word’s basic reference remains an axe used by a carpenter.

This verb means to “prepare” or “make ready.” It describes the act of arranging or equipping something so it is ready for use or for what is about to happen. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, once in Sirach and once in 3 Maccabees. Its exact emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains bringing something into a ready condition.

gl: space one can span with the thumb and little finger; span
d: space one can span with the thumb and little finger; span

e.t: This noun means the distance a person can stretch between the thumb and little finger: a “span.” It names a practical unit for measuring lengths, dimensions, or distances. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across six verses, including descriptions of sacred objects, a weapon-bearing man, and measured features. Its central idea remains a human hand-span used as a clear physical measurement, rather than an abstract idea or personal quality.

This adjective describes someone or something that is hated or abhorred—strongly rejected and regarded with deep dislike. It expresses an intensely negative response rather than mild irritation or ordinary dislike. In the Greek LXX, the word occurs three times, across Isaiah, Daniel, and Wisdom, so its basic meaning is consistent across these writings even though the precise force in each verse depends on its surrounding context. It is a descriptive word applied to whatever is viewed as deeply detestable or loathsome.

This verb means to “sit down together/with”: it describes joining another person or group in a seated position. As a verb, it expresses the act of sitting alongside others rather than merely being present. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, so its basic sense is clear, while its exact force in any one passage comes from the surrounding verse. It appears in Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, and Jeremiah, showing use across several Old Testament settings without changing its central idea.

This Greek LXX noun means “putting together” or “composition”—the combining of parts into a complete arrangement. It can describe something prepared by bringing materials, ingredients, or elements together rather than referring to one individual part. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, with many occurrences in instructions concerning sacred materials and their preparation. Its central idea remains an ordered whole formed through combination.

This Greek LXX noun means “wedge,” an object used to force apart, split, secure, or hold something in place. It names a physical tool or shaped piece rather than an action or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its ordinary meaning remains a wedge: something designed to be driven into or placed between objects.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “bars”—solid pieces used as part of a structure or arrangement. It names a physical object rather than an action or quality. The word occurs four times in the Greek text of the Old Testament, all within 1 Kings 18, where its repeated use indicates the same basic kind of object being mentioned in that passage. Its precise role in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording and context.

This adjective means “of hair” or “made of hair.” It describes something whose material or character is hair, rather than naming the hair itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 26:7, so its precise role there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: it identifies an object or material as hair-based. The word therefore functions as a descriptive term, helping readers recognize what something is made from or what kind of material it involves.

This verb means to drink water. It describes the act of taking water as a beverage, rather than naming a person, object, or general condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 1:12. Its basic meaning is clear from the direct definition, while the surrounding passage determines the particular force of the command or action in that verse.

This adjective means “your,” referring to something that belongs to, comes from, or is associated with the people being addressed. It identifies possession or connection from the speaker’s viewpoint, much like saying “belonging to you.” In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, in Genesis, Proverbs, Amos, and Baruch. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central meaning remains a direct reference to what belongs to those addressed.

This verb describes acting in an overweening or arrogant manner. It portrays a person who exalts himself, carries himself with excessive pride, or treats others from a position of superiority. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here: once in Nehemiah and once in 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense is an attitude expressed through conduct—being presumptuous and self-important rather than humble.

This Greek LXX verb means “send rain” or simply “rain.” It describes the action of rain falling or being sent from above. As a verb, it expresses what the weather does rather than naming the rain itself. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Exodus, including Exodus 9:18 and Exodus 16:4. These references show its use within descriptions of rain, but the precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and its wording.

Chamanim is a noun preserved as the designation “Chamanim.” The word does not come with an expanded English definition here, so its meaning is best stated without adding a guessed interpretation or synonym. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at Ezra 8:27. The supplied lexical information identifies the term itself, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain what Chamanim refers to in that particular passage.

Chattous, also rendered Khattus, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once, in 1 Chronicles 3:22. Because it is a personal name, its meaning is primarily its identifying function: it distinguishes this individual from others in the genealogy. The spelling Chattous reflects one English rendering, while Khattus is another approved rendering of the same name.

This noun means a hoof, specifically a cloven or split hoof. It refers to the hard foot covering of an animal and is used for identifying animals in the dietary instructions recorded in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Leviticus and once in Deuteronomy. Its basic meaning is concrete and physical: the hoof itself, with attention to whether it is divided. The surrounding passage determines how that feature functions in the particular statement.

Chōba, also rendered Khova, is a proper name used for a place in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a geographic location rather than describing an action, quality, or person’s character. This name appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Genesis 14:15 and once in Joshua 19:27. Without the surrounding verse text, the name’s precise location and role cannot be explained further here. The two occurrences show that Chōba is a place designation preserved in separate Old Testament passages.

This Greek LXX noun means “territory” or “estate”—a defined area of land or a possession. It can refer broadly to a region, country, or district, and it may also describe land held as property. The word occurs 220 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing that it is used for both geographical areas and owned land. Its precise sense in any verse depends on whether the surrounding passage speaks about a region or a possession.

This noun refers to a sound that is not formed into recognizable speech—an inarticulate noise or simple sound. It describes the audible noise itself rather than a spoken message or a clearly expressed word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Micah 1:13, and is rendered “sound.” Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a nonverbal or indistinct sound.
